identity.title: Keypad Door Lock Simulation
identity.tagline: Enter the right code, a servo "unlocks" the door. Get it wrong, and the buzzer lets everyone know.

goal: Build a simulated keypad door lock: type a 4-digit code on a membrane keypad, and a servo swings to an "unlocked" position if it matches — with an LCD prompting for input and a buzzer scolding you for a wrong attempt.
simpleSummary: Type a passcode on a keypad to "unlock" a servo-controlled door, with wrong-code buzzing.
howItWorks: A 4x4 membrane keypad has 16 buttons but uses only 8 wires, because it's wired as a grid rather than one wire per button: 4 "row" wires and 4 "column" wires, with each button sitting at the intersection of exactly one row and one column. The Arduino scans this grid by briefly energizing one row at a time and checking which columns respond, which is more wiring-efficient than 16 individual buttons but does need a library (the Keypad library) to handle the scanning logic. From there, the project is just string comparison: build up the digits typed so far, and once four have been entered, compare the result against a fixed correct code.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: Keypad's 4 rows + 4 columns on D2-D9; servo on D10; buzzer on D11; LCD on the I2C bus (A4/A5).

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the keypad's 8 pins (usually a single flat ribbon connector) to Arduino D2 through D9 — rows first (D2-D5), then columns (D6-D9).
wiringSteps.detail: The Keypad library's example sketches list the exact row/column pin order for a standard 4x4 keypad ribbon — matching that order matters, since a swapped row/column produces confusing, seemingly-random wrong readings rather than an obvious failure.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the servo's signal wire to D10, power to 5V, and ground to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: The servo represents the physical lock bolt — rotating to one angle means "locked," another means "unlocked."

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the buzzer between D11 and GND.
wiringSteps.detail: Used here for a short "access denied" beep, not a continuous alarm.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the LCD's I2C backpack: GND to GND, VCC to 5V, SDA to A4, SCL to A5.
wiringSteps.detail: Same LCD wiring used in the Ultrasonic Distance Meter and Temperature & Humidity Display projects.

wiringSteps.instruction: Install the Keypad library alongside LiquidCrystal_I2C and Servo before uploading.
wiringSteps.detail: This project leans on three separate libraries at once — if the sketch won't compile, check that all three installed correctly before assuming it's a wiring problem.

code.explanation: The keypad's getKey() returns the character of whatever key is currently pressed (or a null value if nothing is), so the loop simply ignores empty reads and appends real digits to enteredCode as they arrive. Once four digits are collected, checkCode() runs a plain string comparison (strcmp) against the fixed correct code — a match swings the servo to its "unlocked" angle and automatically re-locks after a few seconds, while a mismatch triggers a short buzzer scold. The '*' key is wired as a manual reset in case of a typo, a small but important usability detail for anything with a fixed-length entry.

expectedBehavior: The LCD prompts for a code and echoes each digit as it's typed. Entering the correct 4 digits shows "Access granted," swings the servo to unlock, and automatically re-locks a few seconds later. Any wrong code shows "Access denied" and sounds a low buzzer tone.

troubleshooting.issue: Keypad presses are read incorrectly or not at all.
troubleshooting.fix: This is almost always rows and columns wired to the wrong pins, or in the wrong order — recheck against the Keypad library's own wiring diagram for a 4x4 matrix, not just the pin count.

troubleshooting.issue: Servo doesn't move, or moves erratically.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the servo has a stable power source — a servo drawing current directly from the same 5V rail as an LCD and buzzer can brown out under load; consider a separate 5V supply if this happens.
Same LCD contrast/address troubleshooting as the Ultrasonic Distance Meter project applies here unchanged.

troubleshooting.issue: Code always seems to fail even when typed correctly.
troubleshooting.fix: Print enteredCode over Serial right before the comparison to see exactly what was captured — a stray leftover character from an incomplete previous entry is the most common cause.

extensions: Add a lockout after 3 failed attempts, requiring a delay before trying again.
Store multiple valid codes (e.g. one per household member) instead of a single fixed code.
Add an RFID card as a second unlock method alongside the keypad (see RFID Access Control).
Log every access attempt (success or failure) with a timestamp over Serial.
